source.title: Classification of rotation-invariant biomedical images using equivariant neural networks
source.authors: Karl Bengtsson Bernander; I. Sintorn; Robin Strand; Ingela Nyström

page_placements.theme: Architecture can change scaling exponents and crossovers

record.tranche_reason: Extends power-law data-scaling analysis to biomedical image classifiers and reports fitted slopes for test error versus training-set size.
record.gate_note: The study tests scaling with training-data amount for biomedical image classifiers, not language-model pretraining loss, parameter count, or compute. Main experiments comparing augmentation, accuracy, and convergence time do not test the listed claim versions; cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study fits a power law to test error against training-set size for two biomedical image classifiers (VGG16 CNN and p4-equivariant GCNN). That is a new-setting result on V5, the power-law form beyond text pretraining. It is weak evidence: the sweep covers about one decade (126–1302 samples), no fit quality or slope uncertainty is reported, and the power-law form is assumed rather than tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude the GCNN reduces test error faster with added data (slope −0.43 vs −0.26). They suggest small-data power-law fits could predict final-model performance and guide architecture and hyperparameter searches, but they do not test this. Their headline claims are equivariance benefits: higher accuracy, faster convergence, and that rotation augmentation can be skipped.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies training-data amount and fits log-log test-error trends for biomedical image classifiers; it does not use language-model pretraining loss, model-size or compute sweeps, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted slopes differ between the CNN and GCNN architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted data-scaling exponent differs by architecture: the equivariant GCNN has k=−0.43 versus k=−0.26 for the CNN with the same weight count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Built-in symmetry (equivariance) steepens the data-scaling exponent of image classifiers on rotation-invariant data.

fits_no_version.finding: At 714 training samples, validation accuracy is 44.06% for the CNN and 74.88% for the GCNN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The equivariant classifier is more data-efficient than the baseline at fixed data amounts.

record.problems: The training-data sweep spans 126 to 1302 samples, and no uncertainty for the fitted power-law slopes is reported. The authors also note possible data leakage in their separate cross-validation setup.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results relevant to the tested power-law scaling version were left out. Main comparisons of augmentation and convergence speed are outside the claim.

untested.parts: Power-law form over several orders of magnitude; scaling in model size or compute; goodness of fit of the power law; other modalities and regimes (video, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer). BloodMNIST was not used in a data sweep.
Not addressed: no language-model pretraining loss.
Extrapolation is only proposed in the Discussion, never tested.
Not addressed for language-model fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The abstract says 'accuracy versus amount of data', but the Results fit test error, which is 1 minus accuracy, not cross-entropy loss. The scaling evidence is a small side experiment within an equivariance study; the main augmentation and convergence experiments are outside the claim. Kaplan et al. is cited only as motivation.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from small-run fits.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Only biomedical image classification with varying training-data amounts was examined; other modalities and regimes, including video, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer, were not tested.
Downstream task performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss.
Language-model scaling-law fit choices, disagreements between published laws, and departures from a single power law.

rows.check: Slope k=−0.26 is from a linear regression on log-log test classification error (not loss) over about one decade of data. No goodness-of-fit, residuals or slope uncertainty are reported, so the power-law form is assumed rather than verified. The baseline is a single-model fit, and its role is architecture comparator.
